policy_title: New ownership model for critical national infrastructure
stated: Reform UK will introduce a new ownership model for critical national infrastructure, bringing 50% of each utility into public ownership and the other 50% owned by UK pension funds, to ensure British taxpayer control and better management. They will also cap standing charges for low users and pensioners.

source.quote: Tighter Regulation and New Ownership Model for Critical National Infrastructure The British taxpayer needs to be in control of Britain’s utilities. Launch a new model that brings 50% of each utility into public ownership. The other 50% would be owned by UK pension funds, benefiting from new expertise and better management. We will ensure standing charges are capped to help low users and pensioners.

bearing_set.reason: Capping standing charges for low users directly reduces energy bills — a core cost-of-living indicator — and the ownership model is justified on grounds of price control and better management, making a real verdict on household energy affordability unavoidable.

The pensioner-specific standing charge cap directly targets a fixed energy cost borne heavily by older people on fixed incomes, with a plausible non-negligible effect on pensioner poverty — an explicit O8 indicator.

Policy explicitly targets 'critical national infrastructure' and frames domestic public/pension ownership as securing 'British taxpayer control', directly bearing on the resilience-to-external-threats indicator under O5.

Acquiring 50% of every utility into public ownership requires substantial capital expenditure (purchase cost or compensation); if funded by borrowing it materially shifts the debt path — a concrete fiscal mechanism.

Replacing private ownership with a public/pension-fund hybrid materially changes the investment and management incentives across critical infrastructure, with genuinely contested effects on long-run productivity and living standards.

Standing charge caps are explicitly targeted at low users and pensioners, narrowing the inequality gap in a major essential cost — a clear distributional mechanism, not merely an aggregate price effect.

membership_note: Four genuine bearings: a direct consumer-price measure (O2) with a distributional tilt (O14), a large public acquisition with fiscal consequences (O12), and a contested governance-of-infrastructure question with long-run productivity implications (O13). Pension-fund ownership could touch O8 but the mechanism for pension adequacy is too speculative and indirect to clear the non-negligible bar without knowing whether the allocation is mandatory or voluntary.
